Need to search first.I've written verse-by-verse notes on 2 Chronicles 24 for every verse except v. 4, but only parts 1 and 2 of your request are well covered. My search tool hit its usage limit early. As a result I couldn't open most full pages, and everything below comes from the excerpts the search returned. Some excerpts didn't say which commentator wrote them, and I've marked those. Fixing the gaps would take a second session (see the end).

**What I couldn't find:**
- Nothing from bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, oca.org, Ligonier, Desiring God, GTY, Seedbed, the Assemblies of God site (ag.org), Pneuma Review, Sam Storms, LCMS or 1517.
- No netbible.org translation notes. I only got its Bible-dictionary entry on Zechariah.
- Nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of v. 20 ("you cannot prosper").

**The two main debates:**
- **Who is the "Zechariah son of Berechiah" in Matthew 23:35?** This draws the widest range of views.
- **Did Joash himself worship idols?** Barnes says the text never charges him with it. Most other writers assume he did.

---

## Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- Joash and Jehoash are the same name. The verse matches 2 Kings 12:1–2 but leaves out the date ("seventh year of Jehu") (Ellicott). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/24-1.htm
- Nothing is known about Zibiah. The Pulpit Commentary assumes her name and home town must have mattered for them to be recorded. Same URL.
- He was hidden six years and crowned at seven, so he was about one year old when his aunt hid him (Clarke). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-chronicles-24.html
- His dates were 835–796 BC, the same time as Jehu of Israel (John Walton, quoted on Precept Austin). Spurgeon notes Joash was the only royal child to survive Athaliah's purge. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-24-commentary

**v. 2**
- The words "all the days of Jehoiada" hint that Joash stopped doing right once Jehoiada died. The chapter then shows that happening (Enduring Word). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-24/
- Kings says Joash did right "while Jehoiada instructed him". Ellicott thinks Chronicles gives the meaning accurately. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-24.html
- Precept Austin stresses two things. "In the sight of the LORD" means God's judgment, not public opinion. Joash's goodness depended on a godly leader, and that didn't last. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-24-commentary

**v. 3**
- Gill says Jehoiada picked wives for Joash, not for himself. He had seen the damage done by Jehoram's marriage to Athaliah and wanted to prevent another bad match. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/24.htm
- An unnamed commentary on Bible Hub notes that a Jewish father was expected to find his son a wife. Jehoiada was acting as Joash's father. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/24-1.htm
- This detail isn't in Kings. Where Chronicles has it, Kings instead mentions that the high places stayed (Ellicott). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-24.html
- Precept Austin's cross-references point to Genesis 4:19 and Matthew 19:4–8, which raises the issue of having two wives. It makes no comment. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64207/

**v. 5**
- Enduring Word says the royal treasury couldn't pay for the work, so Levites were sent to collect. Perhaps they doubted the country towns would give, so they didn't share Joash's urgency. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-24/
- Gill suggests the delay came from the Levites' carelessness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/24.htm
- Ellicott calls this the Chronicler's version of Kings' "each from his acquaintance": local clergy collecting in their own districts. Kings doesn't mention Levites. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-24.html
- Poole gives two readings of "from year to year." Either part of the repair was done each year, or a yearly collection was meant. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/2-chronicles-24.html

**v. 6**
- Ellicott thinks "the tax of Moses" is a general term, not the half-shekel tax of Exodus 30. In Kings, the king's complaint is that the priests kept the money instead of fixing the temple. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-24.html
- Gill calls Jehoiada the chief of the priests and the king's leading minister. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/24.htm
- An 1800s sermon (Irwin) dates the king's rebuke to his 23rd year, after long delay. https://biblehub.com/sermons/auth/irwin/the_repairing_of_the_temple_under_joash_a_missionary_sermon.htm

**v. 7**
- The temple was in ruin because of deliberate attacks, not just age (Enduring Word). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-24/
- Ellicott and Poole say "her sons" probably means Ahaziah, his older brothers and maybe other relatives. Poole adds that they acted at Athaliah's urging, breaking into the treasuries and damaging the building.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-24.html
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/2-chronicles-24.html
- Kingcomments draws a lesson: power pursued for its own sake will hate the service of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/2-chronicles-24.html

**v. 8**
- Enduring Word: even willing givers need to be given a way to give. 2 Kings 12 shows that poor handling of money was part of the problem, and the chest was the fix. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-24/
- Gill refers readers to his notes on 2 Kings 12:9. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/24.htm

**v. 9**
- This verse and the next appear only in Chronicles. Ellicott thinks the Chronicler liked to stress the people's willing giving, as a hint to his own readers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-24.html
- Gill: this was a freewill gift like the one Moses asked for the tabernacle, not a gift to the tabernacle itself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/24.htm

**v. 10**
- Ellicott says the Hebrew means "until they had finished," not "until it was full." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-24.html
- The Pulpit Commentary agrees "till the chest was full" is less likely. It suggests "until everyone that day had given." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/24.htm
- Irwin links the people's joy to "God loveth a cheerful giver." He teaches a fixed, proportional gift plus freewill giving on top. https://biblehub.com/sermons/auth/irwin/the_repairing_of_the_temple_under_joash_a_missionary_sermon.htm
- Precept Austin cross-references 2 Corinthians 9:7. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64207/

**v. 11**
- Pulpit: "daily" means "time after time," not every evening. Levites did the work while the scribe and the priest's officer watched. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/24.htm
- Gill: the "officer" was the high priest's deputy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/24.htm
- Kings has the high priest himself here. Ellicott thinks the Chronicler changed it to protect the high priest's dignity, which mattered more in his own day. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-24.html
- Kingcomments sees king and priest working together as a picture of Christ, the true King-Priest (Zechariah 6:13). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/2-chronicles-24.html

**v. 12**
- Walton: regular upkeep was done by temple staff, but big repairs were hired out. Lists of skilled workers like this one also appear in Assyrian records. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64207/
- Ellicott notes a minor manuscript difference: "doer" versus "doers." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-24.html

**v. 13**
- The Hebrew literally says "a bandage was applied to the work," a picture of healing also used in Nehemiah and Jeremiah (Ellicott). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-24.html
- Bob Utley: "specifications" means David's and Solomon's plans. Precept Austin: God's provision plus faithful work brings lasting restoration. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-24-commentary

**v. 14**
- 2 Kings 12:13–14 says no vessels were made from this money, which seems to clash. Ellicott's answer: Kings describes the money during the repairs, Chronicles the money left over afterwards. Gill gives a similar answer.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-24.html
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/24.htm
- Poole: the new vessels replaced the ones taken by Athaliah's sons. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/2_chronicles/24.htm
- Raymond Dillard: "all the days of Jehoiada" here mirrors v. 2. Together they mark off the good half of the reign. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-24-commentary

**v. 15**
- Enduring Word: Jehoiada's long life showed God's blessing, and God's mercy in holding off Joash's decline. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-24/
- Gill: he was the oldest man recorded since Moses, and ten years older than Moses. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/24.htm
- Ellicott thinks an age of 130 is possible but allows it could be a copying error. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-24.html
- Pulpit sees no sign of a corrupt text. It notes "full of days" is also used of Abraham, Isaac, Job and David. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/24.htm

**v. 16**
- Gill: he was honoured as the man who saved the king and the kingdom, and he was Joash's uncle by marriage. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/24.htm
- Poole: "Israel" here means Judah, the part that still owned God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/2_chronicles/24.htm
- A source quoted on Precept Austin contrasts the two burials: the faithful priest was buried like a king, the privileged king in disgrace. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-24-commentary

**v. 17**
- Readings of what the officials asked for differ:
  - Ellicott: they bowed "as asking a favour," which v. 18 shows was royal approval for idol worship. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-24.html
  - Barnes: the nobles had backed Joash for political reasons. They asked for idols to be tolerated, temple worship carried on, and the king himself isn't charged with idolatry. Keil and Delitzsch say the king didn't dare refuse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/24-17.htm
  - Poole: they asked to worship at the high places, knowing idol worship would then go unnoticed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/2-chronicles-24.html
- Gill: they had secretly leaned toward idols while Jehoiada lived, and now they flattered the king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/24.htm
- Matthew Henry: they flattered him that he had absolute power, and their talk pleased him more than Jehoiada's advice. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_024.cfm
- Pulpit: the word for "bowed" is the one used for worship. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-24.html
- Enduring Word calls Joash a weak man. It quotes Trapp on the flattering courtiers, and an unnamed writer saying Joash gave his heart to Jehoiada, not to God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-24/
- G. Campbell Morgan says the reform was wholly due to Jehoiada. Precept Austin treats the "But" as the hinge of the reign: was Joash's faith his own or borrowed? https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-24-commentary

**v. 18**
- Ellicott: the "wrath" took the form of the Syrian invasion (vv. 23–24). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-24.html
- Poole: it came through Hazael of Syria. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/2_chronicles/24.htm
- Enduring Word: they turned to idols only after leaving God's house, which shows going to the temple had held them back. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-24/

**v. 19**
- Gill: sending prophets showed God's mercy before judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/24.htm
- Henry: no warning or threat moved them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_024.cfm
- Enduring Word: refusing the prophets was a worse sin than the idolatry itself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-24/

**v. 20**
- "Came upon" literally means "clothed." "The priest" refers to Jehoiada, not Zechariah (Ellicott). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/24-20.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown think Zechariah was probably a younger son, since he isn't in the high-priest list. Same URL.
- Pulpit: "son" may mean grandson, given Jehoiada's age. Also, the Hebrew reads "you will not prosper." Same URL.
- Gill: he stood on a raised platform like Ezra's. Turning to idols blocks prosperity of body and soul. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/24.htm
- Enduring Word: the Chronicler includes the "forsaken" principle because it mattered to the returned exiles who first read the book. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-24/
- Gaebelein: Zechariah was the king's cousin, and his words echo 2 Chronicles 15:2 (excerpt on StudyLight was in Spanish). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/24-20.html
- Precept Austin: he speaks with God's authority, not his own anger. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-24-commentary

**v. 21**
- Ellicott notes the irony that stoning was the Law's penalty for idolatry. He thinks Zechariah's words were probably passed off as treason. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-24.html
- Constable: Zechariah died in the same courtyard where Joash was anointed, and Jehoiada had kept murder out of the temple. He compares Naboth's stoning. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/24-21.html
- Poole: "they" means the people, led astray by the king and officials. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/2-chronicles-24.html
- Clarke: when a man falls from God, he is capable of any cruelty. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/24-21.html

**v. 22**
- John Olley points out a pun. Joash "did not remember" (Hebrew *zakar*), while Zechariah's name means "the LORD has remembered." https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-24-commentary
- Readings of the dying words differ:
  - Ellicott sets them against Stephen's prayer of forgiveness, and sees them as a prophecy soon fulfilled. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-24.html
  - Pulpit prefers the reading "The LORD will see and will require." That makes it a statement, not a prayer, echoing Genesis 9:5. The Pulpit's study notes add that it wasn't spoken in an unforgiving spirit.
    - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/24.htm
    - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-24.html
  - Gill: they weren't spoken from personal revenge, but for the honour of God's justice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/24.htm
- Henry calls ingratitude the worst thing you can say of a man. He repeats a Jewish tradition that the murder broke seven laws at once, including killing a priest, a prophet and a judge. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_024.cfm

**Side debate: Zechariah in Matthew 23:35** ("Zechariah son of Berechiah")
- **It's this Zechariah; the father had two names:**
  - Calvin (Reformed) suggests "Barachiah" may have been a title of honour for Jehoiada. He also mentions Jerome's view that it is a copying mistake. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/23-35.html
  - Wesley (Methodist) says simply that Barachiah is the one called Jehoiada in 2 Chronicles. Same URL.
  - Gill (Baptist) rules out the later prophet Zechariah, since the temple and altar weren't yet rebuilt in his day. Same URL.
  - Gaebelein holds the same view. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/24-20.html
- **Berechiah was the father and Jehoiada the grandfather:** Ellicott, Pulpit and Constable all allow this. Constable adds that Chronicles ended the Hebrew Bible, so "Abel to Zechariah" means "all the martyrs from first to last." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-24.html and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/23-35.html
- **A copying error:** one older commentary (Preacher's Homiletical) notes the words "son of Barachias" are missing from the Sinaitic manuscript and from Luke 11:51, and may have been added later. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/23-35.htm
- **A slip or confusion by the writer:** Barclay calls it a slip by the Gospel writer. Dummelow says the name was confused with the prophet Zechariah's.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/23-35.html
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/24-20.html
- **Catholic:** the Catholic Encyclopedia on catholic.com says the prophet Zechariah is very unlikely to be meant; Jesus means the son of Joiada. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/zacharias
  - Haydock's Catholic commentary reports Jerome found "son of Joiada" in the Gospel of the Nazarenes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/23-35.html
- **Other views:** Smith's Bible Dictionary (on netbible.org) says many Greek Church Fathers took it to mean John the Baptist's father. Smith himself sides with Jehoiada's son. https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=ZECHARIAH
  - GotQuestions presents the Jehoiada identification as what "some scholars assume." https://www.gotquestions.org/prophet-Zechariah.html

**v. 23**
- Poole: "at the end of the year" shows how fast God answered the prophet's blood. The officials were killed because they started the apostasy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/2_chronicles/24.htm
- Ellicott: a small Syrian detachment beat a large army led by Judah's officials, and seems to have targeted the leaders. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-24.html
- Pulpit suggests news of Zechariah's murder may have prompted Hazael's raid. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/24.htm
- Gill is unsure whether this is the same campaign as 2 Kings 12:17. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/24.htm
- Enduring Word: the officials who misled Joash were the ones destroyed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-24/

**v. 24**
- Ellicott:
  - "Executed judgment" is always used of God's punishment.
  - Kings adds that Joash paid off Hazael with temple treasures.
  - Chronicles tells the story to draw a moral lesson.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-24.html
- Gill: the Syrians were God's tools of judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/24.htm
- Precept Austin's heading here: past faithfulness doesn't cancel present rebellion. Like Assyria and Babylon later, a foreign army carried out God's justice. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-24-commentary

**v. 25**
- Readings of Joash's condition differ:
  - Gill says he was wounded. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/24.htm
  - Ellicott says the text doesn't say Joash was wounded, and the sickness may have come from the disaster. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/24-25.htm
  - An unnamed excerpt on the same page says God struck him with disease of body or mind or both. Same URL.
- Pulpit: he was so ill and bedridden that his servants had an easy chance. Their act wasn't necessarily pious zeal; God's providence moved them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/24.htm
- Poole: "sons" (plural, in older versions) stands for one son. Gill allows more than one may have been killed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/2-chronicles-24.html
- Enduring Word: a bitter irony, since Joash was denied the royal tombs that Jehoiada received, and never repented. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-24/

**v. 26**
- Whitelaw (Pulpit): led astray by those who should have served him, Joash was killed by his actual servants. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-24.html
- A source quoted on Precept Austin suggests the killers' foreign mothers are a reminder of the danger of foreign worship. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-24-commentary

**v. 27**
- Keil and Delitzsch record different readings of the word the BSB translates "pronouncements":
  - The Vulgate and Luther took it as the Moses tax.
  - Some took it as the tribute paid to Syria.
  - Keil, following Clericus, prefers prophetic warnings against Joash.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/24-25.htm
- Poole: either harsh prophecies or God's judgments. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/2-chronicles-24.html
- Clarke: probably the Syrian tribute. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-chronicles-24.html
- Guzik takes it as the warnings of vv. 19–20. https://blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/studyguide_2ch/2ch_24.cfm

---

## Do Protestant traditions really differ?

Mostly no. Every source I found, whether Baptist (Gill), Puritan (Henry, Poole), Anglican (Ellicott, Pulpit), Methodist (Wesley) or Calvary Chapel (Guzik/Enduring Word), reads the chapter the same way: a good start that depended on another man's faith, apostasy, and fitting judgment. The real disagreements are between individual writers, not traditions:
- Whether Joash personally worshipped idols (Barnes says the text doesn't say so).
- Whether Zechariah's last words were a curse or a prophecy.
- Who is meant in Matthew 23:35.

Henry's line "It is easier to build temples, than to be temples to God" is a common application (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/24-1.htm).

To fill the gaps, a second session could target enduringword.com's full page, newadvent.org, bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org's 2 Chronicles 24 notes, and the Reformed, Lutheran and Pentecostal sites listed above.
